DOCUMENT:
Briefing: Moving All Council Services to a Four-Day Week

1. Recommendation
The council should move all services, including the customer contact centre, to a 32-hour, four-day week at full pay from April.

2. Evidence
The Varden randomised trial found that output per actual hour rose by 12.5% after nine months in case-processing offices, and by 8.5% at 24 months. Actual hours fell by 11%. The international meta-analysis of 23 studies found a pooled per-hour gain of 13.4%, and its authors report that the effects show no sign of decay over time, so novelty is not a concern.

3. Output per worker
Because the per-hour gain (8.5%) is close to the hours cut, and the meta-analysis figure (13.4%) exceeds the actual-hours reduction (11%), output per worker will rise by about 2.4% (13.4% minus 11%).

4. Wellbeing
Sickness absence fell by about a third and resignations roughly halved in the trial offices. These savings come on top of the productivity gain.

5. Contact centre
The contact centre will follow the same model as the other services. Staff will cover the same opening hours on a rota.

6. Conclusion
The evidence supports a council-wide four-day week with no loss of output and substantial wellbeing gains.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "output per worker will rise by about 2.4% (13.4% minus 11%)" -- Per-worker change is multiplicative (1.134 x 0.89 = 1.009, about +0.9%, not +2.4%), and the 13.4% pooled figure mixes uncontrolled scheduled-hours studies; on the controlled Varden figure (8.5%) output per worker falls about 3.4% (1.085 x 0.89).
2. [misread_evidence] at: "its authors report that the effects show no sign of decay over time, so novelty is not a concern" -- The meta-analysis's no-decay claim rested on four uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours; the briefing's own Varden figures (12.5% at nine months, 8.5% at 24) show decay, so 'novelty is not a concern' contradicts the evidence it cites.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "The contact centre will follow the same model as the other services. Staff will cover the same opening hours on a rota." -- The contact centre is coverage-bound work (output tied to presence). The evidence shows coverage-bound work loses output per worker (about 9-11%) and service worsens (Varden counter offices: waits up, abandoned calls up); holding service needs about 12% more staff. The briefing ignores this.

REVIEW:
# Review: *Briefing: Moving All Council Services to a Four-Day Week*

The sources are the right ones, but the briefing misstates what they found. The central claim, that output per worker rises and every service comes out ahead, is wrong. The sources show output per worker falling slightly in office-based work and clearly in the contact centre. As written, the recommendation is not supported by the evidence it cites.

## 1. The output-per-worker arithmetic is wrong (section 3)

The briefing subtracts percentages and takes the per-hour figure from one source and the hours figure from another. Output per worker is output per hour multiplied by hours per worker:

| Inputs | Calculation | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|
| Varden at 24 months (the briefing's own figures) | 1.085 × 0.89 = 0.966 | **−3.4%** |
| Meta-analysis per-hour figure with Varden hours (mixing sources) | 1.134 × 0.89 = 1.009 | +0.9% |
| Meta-analysis's own per-worker estimate | as reported | **−1.8%** (CI −4.9 to +1.4) |

The section undercuts itself. It says the 8.5% per-hour gain is "close to the hours cut" of 11%. But a per-hour gain smaller than the hours cut means output per worker falls. The author's note says the per-hour gain is larger than the hours cut; in Varden's data it isn't.

The 13.4% figure is also the wrong one to use. It is the pooled estimate across all 23 studies, and the meta-analysis itself shows it is inflated by uncontrolled studies and by dividing output by scheduled rather than actual hours. Its better-measured estimates are:

- controlled studies of office-type work: +9.6% per hour, −2.7% per worker;
- adjusted for small-study bias: +9.1% per hour.

## 2. The contact centre is where the evidence is clearest, and it points the other way (section 5)

The briefing proposes covering the same opening hours on a rota. That is exactly what Varden did in its counter and contact-centre offices:

- output per worker fell 11.4% (CI −16.9 to −5.9);
- average waits rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes, and abandoned calls from 6% to 10%;
- the county ended that arm at month 12, when waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices;
- restoring service was estimated to need 12% more staff, raising cost per contact by about 9%.

The meta-analysis agrees. Per-worker output fell about 9% across seven studies of shift- and counter-based work, consistently (I² = 22%). This is the most consistent finding in the evidence.

A single council-wide policy may be simpler, and treating staff equally is a legitimate goal. But the briefing has to state the cost of that choice: either longer waits for residents, or more staff for the contact centre. As written it implies there is no cost.

## 3. The evidence section misstates three findings (section 2)

- **"12.5% … and 8.5% at 24 months."** These come from different measures. The 12.5% divides output by timesheet hours; the 8.5% divides by time logged on the case-management system. On the same timesheet measure the gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8%.
- **"No sign of decay, so novelty is not a concern."** The meta-analysis's no-decay claim rested on four longer studies, all uncontrolled and all using scheduled hours. The Varden 24-month report showed this and found a real decline. Novelty is still an open concern.
- **The 11% fall in hours applies to Varden's case-processing offices only.** It shouldn't be read as the expected reduction for every service.

## 4. The wellbeing figures are overstated (section 4)

- **Sickness absence fell 27%, about a quarter, not a third.** Part of the fall is mechanical: a four-day week leaves fewer scheduled days on which anyone can be off sick.
- **Resignations were 4.1% against 7.9% a year.** That is roughly halved, but there were few resignations, so the estimate is imprecise.
- **"Savings on top of the productivity gain."** There is no per-worker productivity gain to add savings to. And no source estimates what these wellbeing improvements are worth in money.

## 5. The conclusion goes beyond the evidence (sections 1 and 6)

- **"No loss of output" is not supported.**
  - For office-type work, the evidence suggests a small loss (−3.4%), though one consistent with no change.
  - For the contact centre, it shows a clear loss.
- **"All services" goes beyond the evidence.**
  - The strongest evidence comes from one county's case-processing and counter offices, with only seven offices in each group.
  - Field services, care rotas and shift work are barely studied, and the meta-analysis groups care rotas with other coverage work where output fell.
- **The scheme differs from Varden's.** Varden cut scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30. A 32-hour week is a different cut, from a baseline the briefing doesn't state.
- **Cost is missing.**
  - With full pay and output per worker 2–4% lower, unit labour cost rises by about the same amount in office-type work.
  - Overtime adds to that.
  - The contact centre adds roughly 9% if staffed to maintain service.

## 6. What the briefing leaves out that the board would want

- **About half of Varden's gain came from cutting recurring meetings.** In the one trial that tested this, fewer meetings accounted for roughly 47% of the per-hour gain. Some of that benefit might be available without changing hours, by auditing meetings now.
- **Two problems to monitor:**
  - work spilling into overtime;
  - case backlogs building up behind stable completion figures.

## A recommendation the evidence would support

> Pilot a four-day week in case-processing and back-office services, with a comparison group of services that keep current hours, and track actual hours, backlogs and cost per case. Do not include the contact centre unless the board accepts longer waits or funds about 12% more staff (around 9% higher cost per contact). Run a recurring-meeting audit across all services now, since roughly half the measured gain came through fewer meetings.

I can redraft the full briefing on this basis, keeping it about the same length.
